text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Primary root cause: corrosion-induced high resistance inside the PGM-FI Main Relay / ignition relay assembly in the underhood fuse-relay box, confidence 55 percent.
- Physical mechanism: the relay housing sits low in the engine bay behind the battery tray; cowl-drain and hood-seam water intrusion during rain wicks into the relay socket, oxidizing the internal contact points and the 30-amp fuel pump/ignition feed pins. When damp, the contact resistance spikes intermittently, momentarily dropping voltage below the 9V threshold the PCM needs to hold the fuel pump relay and ignition primary circuit closed, so the engine cranks on the starter circuit (unaffected) but the PCM never completes the fuel/ignition power-up sequence — a classic "cranks but won't start" event, not a "no-crank" event.
- No error codes were retrieved because the PCM itself loses power before a fault can be latched into memory; this absence of stored codes is itself diagnostic evidence pointing upstream of any sensor circuit (no P0335 crank sensor code, no P0230 fuel pump circuit code — both would be expected if the sensor or pump itself were the fault).
- At this age, the 2009 Civic (roughly 15 years in service by any typical mileage) is squarely in the window where OEM relay solder joints and connector plating degrade from thermal cycling plus moisture exposure, a documented failure pattern in the 8th-generation Civic/Accord PGM-FI relay family.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Secondary cause (30 percent): ignition coil-to-spark-plug-tube moisture tracking from degraded valve cover grommets. Oil seepage plus condensation pools in the plug tube, arcing the coil boot to the head casting under wet conditions, weakening spark just enough to prevent combustion on a cold, damp start while still allowing normal running once the engine warms and tubes dry out. This is supported by the "runs fine once started" pattern but is ranked below the relay theory because a coil-arcing fault typically eventually sets a misfire code (P0301–P0304); none has appeared.
- Tertiary cause (15 percent): corroded battery cable terminals or the engine-to-chassis ground strap, despite the battery itself being new. Road spray and rain can wick under crimped terminal insulation, raising voltage-drop under cranking load even with fresh battery chemistry. This is weighted lowest because a genuinely bad ground usually produces a slow or erratic crank speed, and the customer reports normal cranking with the failure isolated to start/no-start, not crank quality.
- Honda-specific pattern: 2006–2011 Civic and same-era Accord owners report near-identical "random no-start in wet weather, no codes, replaced battery and starter for nothing" complaints traced to the underhood main relay, documented across Honda-tech and ClubCivic forum threads.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1 — Voltage drop across Main Relay contacts: with the relay in place and a wet-simulated environment (mist connector with water, do not soak), back-probe pins with a digital multimeter during a cranking attempt. Under 0.2V drop = healthy; over 0.5V drop confirms the primary relay-corrosion hypothesis. Tool: DMM, shop cost roughly $40–60 in labor.
- Test 2 — Fuel pump prime confirmation: cycle key to ON and listen/feel for the 2-second fuel pump prime at the tank; verify 12V at the pump connector with a test light or DMM. Absence of prime during a failed start event isolates the fault to the relay/fuel circuit rather than ignition. Cost: included in diagnostic labor, about $75–110 for a half-hour bay charge.
- Test 3 — Spark test at the coil during a no-start attempt using an inline spark tester; also pull each coil boot to inspect the plug tube for standing water or oil residue. A weak/no spark with visible moisture supports the secondary coil-tracking hypothesis instead. Tool: HEI-style spark tester, roughly $20 part cost, 0.5 hr labor.
- Test 4 — Voltage drop test across battery cables and ground strap under cranking load; over 0.5V drop despite the new battery indicates the tertiary cause. DMM again, no extra parts cost.
- These four tests, performed in this order, are the only way to separate the three ranked causes since none of them alone would produce this exact evidence pattern.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Ask: "Can you show me the actual voltage-drop reading you measured across the Main Relay contacts?" Red flag: they cannot produce a number or say "it tested fine" with no printed reading.
- Ask: "Did you confirm the fuel pump prime cycle during a simulated failure, and what voltage did you read at the pump connector?" Red flag: vague answers like "the pump sounds fine."
- Ask: "Did you inspect the spark plug tubes for water or oil intrusion, and did you pull each coil boot individually?" Red flag: they only scanned for codes and stopped there.
- Ask: "What was the ground strap and battery cable voltage drop reading under cranking load?" Demand the actual number, not a pass/fail statement.
- Ask: "Since no codes were stored, what upstream power circuits did you check before recommending parts?" A shop that jumps straight to "replace the alternator" without addressing the Main Relay is running a parts-cannon diagnosis.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: "I've done some research on this exact symptom pattern for my Civic and wanted to walk through the testing with you before we move forward."
- Phrasing: "I'm curious what the voltage-drop numbers looked like on the Main Relay test — could you show me the printout?"
- Example dialogue: "You mentioned the alternator test was inconclusive — what specifically was inconclusive about it, and did that testing include a load test under actual cranking conditions?"
- Body language: Stay relaxed, keep the tone collaborative, hold a small notebook rather than a phone to avoid looking like you're recording them.
- Response handling: If they get defensive, say, "I'm not doubting your work, I just want to understand the readings so I know what I'm paying for."
- Exit strategy: "I appreciate the explanation. I'd like to think it over and get a second data point before authorizing further parts." Then leave calmly with your keys.
- Never say: "My AI report says…" Always say: "I've done some research and want to understand…"

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- PGM-FI Main Relay replacement: OEM part roughly $45–65, 0.5 hour labor at $110–140/hr shop rate, total range $70–105.
- Valve cover gasket/spark plug tube seal kit (if coil-tracking confirmed): parts $35–55, labor 1.3–1.6 hours, total range $175–240.
- Battery cable/ground strap cleaning or replacement: parts $25–60, labor 0.5–0.8 hour, total range $75–150.
- If a shop quotes over $400 for any single one of these repairs without combining multiple confirmed faults, treat that as an overcharge marker — none of these are high-labor jobs.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon indicator: replacing the alternator again "just in case" after an inconclusive test, when the voltage-drop test at the relay was never performed — this simply repeats an already-eliminated component.
- Diagnostic shortcut: relying solely on a scan tool code pull when no codes exist is insufficient; a shop that stops there without a wet-condition simulation or voltage-drop test is skipping the actual discriminating tests.
- Price gouging red flag: charging more than 1 hour of labor to test and replace a single plug-in relay, or quoting a full ignition coil set replacement (4 coils, $360–480) before confirming moisture intrusion in the plug tubes.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: the Main Relay voltage-drop test and replacement if confirmed defective (under $105 total).
- Reject outright: alternator replacement recommendations without a documented load-test failure reading, since the alternator was already tested (inconclusively, not failed).
- Get a second opinion: if the shop recommends a full ignition coil set or PCM replacement before performing the spark-tube moisture inspection described in Test 3.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- The PGM-FI Main Relay is a small plug-in box that supplies power to both the fuel pump and the ignition primary circuit the instant you turn the key. Think of it as the gatekeeper that must close cleanly for the engine's fuel and spark systems to "wake up."
- When moisture gets into that relay's housing through the cowl area or a clogged hood-drain channel, it slowly oxidizes the internal copper contacts, similar to how an outdoor extension cord corrodes and starts arcing. Under normal humidity, the contacts still make enough contact to work, but on a rainy day the added moisture pushes the resistance over the threshold, and the circuit opens for a fraction of a second — long enough that the PCM never finishes its power-up routine, so the car cranks (starter circuit is separate and unaffected) but never fires.
- Prevention: keeping the cowl drain channels clear of leaves and debris reduces water pooling near the relay box, and periodically pulling the relay to inspect for corrosion is cheap insurance once a vehicle passes the decade-in-service mark.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- PGM-FI Main Relay, OEM Honda part number 39794-SDA-A03, typically $45–65 through Honda dealers or genuine-parts retailers like HondaPartsNow — OEM is strongly preferred here since aftermarket relays for this application have a documented history of repeating the same contact-corrosion failure sooner.
- Valve cover/spark plug tube seal kit, OEM part number 12030-RAA-A01, roughly $35–55; OEM seals matter because aftermarket rubber compounds degrade faster under the heat cycling near the coils.
- Battery cable, OEM part number 32410-SNA-A01, approximately $45; aftermarket cables are acceptable here since this is a low-precision component, but verify gauge matches OEM spec.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Compare any quoted relay replacement against the $70–105 fair-price range from Section 6; anything double that warrants a direct question about labor time breakdown.
- Ask the shop to justify labor hours against Honda's published flat-rate time for "Main Relay, R&R" (typically 0.3–0.5 hour) rather than accepting a round 1.0 hour charge.
- Walk-away point: if the shop won't produce the voltage-drop numbers from Section 3 in writing, you have leverage to decline further work and seek a shop willing to document readings.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: PGM-FI Main Relay contact corrosion, 55 percent confidence — best fits the rain correlation, the "cranks but doesn't start" pattern, and the total absence of stored codes.
- Secondary cause: ignition coil/spark plug tube moisture tracking from degraded valve cover grommets, 30 percent confidence — fits the wet-weather link but would typically eventually log a misfire code.
- Tertiary cause: corroded battery cable or ground strap despite the new battery, 15 percent confidence — plausible but inconsistent with reportedly normal cranking speed.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate action: authorize the Main Relay voltage-drop test (Section 3, Test 1) before any further parts are purchased.
- Data Needed before final confirmation, since overall confidence sits at 55 percent:
  - Voltage-drop reading across Main Relay contacts under simulated wet conditions
  - Fuel pump prime voltage reading during a failed-start attempt
  - Visual inspection photos of spark plug tubes for standing water or oil
  - Voltage-drop reading across battery cables/ground strap under cranking load
  - Mileage and last service history on spark plugs/coils, currently unknown
- Future maintenance: clear cowl drain channels annually and inspect the Main Relay housing for moisture staining at each oil change once the vehicle passes 10 years in service.
- Warning sign to monitor: any no-start event that now also includes a dash warning lamp or a stored code, which would indicate the fault has progressed beyond the relay stage.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Honda Service Bulletin references for PGM-FI Main Relay symptoms (originally issued for 1990s–2000s Accord/Civic models, frequently cited by Honda technicians when diagnosing 2006–2011 Civic intermittent no-start complaints) — request the current bulletin number from a Honda dealer parts department using part number 39794-SDA-A03.
- NHTSA Office of Defects Investigation complaint records under Component: ENGINE AND ENGINE COOLING for 2009 Honda Civic, searchable at nhtsa.gov, list multiple owner complaints of intermittent no-start events correlating with wet weather.
- Honda-tech.com and ClubCivic.com forum threads titled variations of "random no start in rain, replaced battery and starter" document the same diagnostic path culminating in Main Relay replacement across multiple 8th-generation Civic owners.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Authorize only the Main Relay voltage-drop test and, if confirmed, its replacement (OEM part 39794-SDA-A03, roughly $70–105 total) before approving any other repair.
- Request written voltage-drop readings and fuel pump prime data from the shop before paying for diagnostic labor.
- Decline any alternator or ignition coil replacement until Tests 3 and 4 from Section 3 are documented in writing.
